questions.question:
The value of [latex]x [/latex] such that [latex]x > 1 [/latex], satisfying the equation
[latex]  \int_{1}^{x}t \ln t \, dt = \frac{1}{4} [/latex] is
questions.explanation:
Integrate by parts: with [latex]u=\ln t,\ dv=t\,dt[/latex] (so [latex]du=dt/t,\ v=t^2/2[/latex]):
[latex]\int t\ln t\,dt=\dfrac{t^2}2\ln t-\int\dfrac{t}2\,dt=\dfrac{t^2}2\ln t-\dfrac{t^2}4[/latex]

Evaluating from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]x[/latex]: [latex]\left(\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4\right)-\left(0-\dfrac14\right)=\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4+\dfrac14[/latex]

Setting this equal to [latex]\dfrac14[/latex]: [latex]\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4=0\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{x^2}2\left(\ln x-\dfrac12\right)=0[/latex]
Since [latex]x>1[/latex] means [latex]x^2\ne0[/latex], we need [latex]\ln x=\dfrac12\ \Rightarrow\ x=e^{1/2}=\sqrt e[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\sqrt{e}[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider the systems,each consisting of m linear equations in n variables.
I. If m [latex]\lt[/latex] n, then all such systems have a solution
II. If m [latex]\gt[/latex] n, then none of these systems has a solution
III. If m = n, then there exists a system which has a solution
Which one of the following is CORRECT?

options.A: I, II and III are true
options.B: Only II and III are true

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- I: m [latex]\lt[/latex] n does not guarantee a solution: x + y = 1 and x + y = 2 are inconsistent [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- II: m [latex]\gt[/latex] n systems can have solutions (e.g. the same equation repeated) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- III: with m = n, the homogeneous system Ax = 0 always has x = 0 as a solution [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Only III is true

(ii) Subtract the third column from the first column.

questions.explanation:
Adding a row to another row, or subtracting a column from another column, does not change the determinant.

In the original matrix the third column is 15 times the first (45 = 15 [latex]\times[/latex] 3, 105 = 15 [latex]\times[/latex] 7, 195 = 15 [latex]\times[/latex] 13), so the determinant is 0.

Answer: 0

questions.question:
The weight of a sequence [latex]a_{0},a_{1},...,a_{n-1}[/latex] of real numbers is defined as [latex]a_{0}+a_{1}/2+...+a_{n-1}/2^{n-1}[/latex] A subsequence of a sequence is obtained by deleting some elements from the sequence, keeping the order of the remaining elements
the same. Let X denote the maximum possible weight of a subsequence of
[latex]a_{0},a_{1},...,a_{n-1}[/latex] and Y the maximum possible weight of a subsequence of [latex]a_{0},a_{1},...,a_{n-1}[/latex]. Then X is equal to
questions.explanation:
Either a0 is not taken: the best weight comes from the rest, i.e. Y.

Or a0 is taken: a0 gets weight 1 and the rest of the chosen subsequence shifts one place, so its weights halve: [latex]a_0+Y/2[/latex].

X = max(Y, [latex]a_0+Y/2[/latex])

Answer: max(Y, [latex]a_0[/latex] + Y/2)

questions.question: Let [latex]A[/latex]  be an [latex] n \times n[/latex]  matrix over the set of all real numbers [latex]R[/latex]. Let [latex]B[/latex]  be a matrix obtained from [latex]A[/latex] by swapping two rows. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.A: The determinant of [latex]B[/latex] is the negative of the determinant of [latex]A[/latex]
options.B: If [latex]A[/latex] is invertible, then [latex]B[/latex] is also invertible
options.C: If [latex]A[/latex] is symmetric, then [latex]B[/latex] is also symmetric
options.D: If the trace of [latex]A[/latex] is zero, then the trace of [latex]B[/latex] is also zero

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Swapping two rows changes the sign of the determinant: [latex]\det B=-\det A[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- So [latex]\det A\ne0\Rightarrow\det B\ne0[/latex]: B is invertible [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{bmatrix}[/latex] is symmetric, but [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}[/latex] is not [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex] has trace 0, but [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}[/latex] has trace 1 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

questions.question:
Let [latex]A[/latex] be a 2x2 matrix as given:
[latex]A = \left[\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{array}\right][/latex]
What are the eigenvalues of the matrix [latex]A^{13}[/latex]?
questions.explanation:
Find the eigenvalues of [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex] from its characteristic equation:
[latex](1-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)-1\times1=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda^2-1-1=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda^2=2\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=\pm\sqrt2[/latex]

If [latex]\lambda[/latex] is an eigenvalue of [latex]A[/latex], then [latex]\lambda^{13}[/latex] is the corresponding eigenvalue of [latex]A^{13}[/latex] (eigenvalues of a matrix power are just the original eigenvalues raised to that power):
[latex](\sqrt2)^{13}=2^{13/2}=2^{6}\cdot2^{1/2}=64\sqrt2[/latex], and similarly [latex](-\sqrt2)^{13}=-64\sqrt2[/latex].

Answer: 64√2, -64√2

questions.question:
Let [latex]f(x)=x^{-(1/3)}[/latex] and A denote the area of the region bounded by f(x) and the x-axis, when x varies from -1 to 1. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
I) f is continuous in [-1,1]
II) f is not bounded in [-1,1]
III) A is nonzero and finite
questions.explanation:
[latex]f(x)=x^{-1/3}[/latex] blows up at x = 0, so it is not continuous (I false) and not bounded (II true) on [[latex]-[/latex]1, 1].

Area = [latex]2\int_0^1x^{-1/3}dx=2\cdot\frac32=3[/latex], finite and non-zero (III true).

Answer: II and III only
